newsitem.title: USA: House tax panel chief says premature for tax talks.
newsitem.headline: House tax panel chief says premature for tax talks.

text.p: Key lawmakers Tuesday accused the administration of holding back information needed to evaluate President Clinton's tax plan, and said bipartisan tax talks could not get under way until it was received.

Rep. Bill Archer, the Texas Republican who chairs the House Ways and Means Committee where all tax legislation must originate, said it was premature to start tax negotiations with the White House until the Treasury provided more details about Clinton's proposals.
"I don't see how we can begin to talk about negotiating a tax bill until we have the specificity of their tax proposals," Archer said during a tax conference.

He and Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican, sent Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin a letter seeking specifics on how the president's proposed tax cuts would be phased out if necessary to raise more money to balance the budget.
Clinton's 1998 budget proposes a $98 billion tax cut over five years.
The lawmakers said the Joint Committee on Taxation needed that information to assess the effect of Clinton's proposal on revenues accurately.
"They've got to define their tax provisions. They can't just simply allude to them in generalities if we're to be able to get tax estimates on them," Archer said.
A Treasury spokesman had no immediate comment.

Earlier, a White House aide at the same conference had said it was hoped that the bipartisan working groups on five key issues including taxes could begin next week. The working groups were formed after Clinton met Congressional leaders to discuss priorities for this year, and the tax group includes Archer, Rubin and Roth.
"We hope to start all the working groups as early as next week," John Hilley, assistant to the President and White House director of legislative affairs, said.
Archer said he expected the final budget to provide tax cuts for capital gains, estates and families and also to include provisions to expand individual retirement accounts.
"I think all of those will be part of the ultimate tax package," Archer said.
He said he hoped negotiations with the administration would begin "reasonably soon."

Republicans and the White House stuck to the positions they have staked out on a capital gains tax cut. Republicans say a capital gains tax cut should be broad-based, while Clinton has proposed targeting it only for home sales.
"We have a capital gains tax cut proposal on the table ... At this time, we are unwilling to move off that," Hilley of the White House said.
Rep. Tom DeLay, a member of the Republican leadership as House Whip, said Republicans were also holding their position.
"We're going to hold our position, too," DeLay of Texas said. Although he said he was heartened that Senate Democratic leaders were coming up with their own capital gains tax cut proposals.
"I am really looking forward to that and we have to be excited about the fact that maybe we actually will start to do something about the taxes on capital," DeLay said.
